newsitem.title: UK: Bees have royal blood too, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Bees have royal blood too, study finds.

text.p: Bees have royal blood lines just like the great royal families of Europe or Japan, entomologists reported on Wednesday.
When a queen bee dies, her successor will be her own daughter as only queen bees have offspring. But the researchers found the successor is likely to have had a "royal" father as well.

Robin Moritz of the Technische Universitat Berlin and Mike Allsopp of the Plant Protection Research Institute in Stellenbosch, South Africa, studied Cape honey bees to find out how they managed their royal successions.
They took two colonies and killed the queen bees, then split each colony in half.
Queen bees mate with many of the males in a hive, but Mortiz's group discovered the family lines of most males died out after a few weeks.
The same families tended to survive in all four colonies, they found. The females who took over as queen came from these dominant lines.
Moritz and his colleagues explained why the royal bees did not simply take over the entire colony and its reproduction. Just like human society, a class of common workers is vital.

"Colonies composed of dominant workers alone are unable to produce any fertile offspring because there are no subordinate workers to tend to the brood or to rear adults," they wrote in a letter to the science journal Nature.
